title: Be opened (Mark 7:31–37)
hookLine: he puts fingers in a deaf man's ears, sighs, and says ephphatha
last: EVEN THE DOGS EAT THE CRUMBS.

cards: Jesus takes the long way back. In the King James text he leaves the coasts of Tyre and Sidon and comes to the Sea of Galilee through the ten cities, the Decapolis, where the man called Legion went home to tell his story.
Maybe that's why people there bring someone to him: a man who is deaf and can hardly speak. They beg Jesus to lay his hand on him.
What Jesus does next is so physical, so hands-on, that some readers find it almost awkward. Mark keeps every gesture, and one Aramaic word.

teach.h: TAKEN ASIDE, AWAY FROM THE CROWD.
teach.b: First, Jesus takes the man aside, away from the crowd. No show, just the two of them. Then he speaks the man's language, the language of touch.
He puts his fingers in the man's ears. He spits and touches his tongue.
Then, in the old King James Bible, "looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened." He sighed: a groan, a deep breath out. Mark doesn't explain it.
Some hear compassion, some hear prayer, some hear grief at all the ways the world is closed. Ephphatha is Aramaic, like talitha koum, and Mark translates it: be opened.
"And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain."

teach.h: HE HATH DONE ALL THINGS WELL.
teach.b: The crowd can't keep quiet about it: "He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak." Dumb is the old word for unable to speak.
Readers who know the prophet Isaiah hear his promise that one day the ears of the deaf would be unstopped and the tongue of the mute would sing. And the word lives on in church.

In the Catholic baptism rite, the priest may touch the ears and mouth of the newly baptized and say ephphatha, praying that they'll soon hear God's word and speak it. That closes a week. Sheep without a shepherd.
It is I. Wherever he went. Tradition.
What comes out. Crumbs under the table. And one word, sighed toward heaven: be opened.

how: In the Catholic rite of baptism, the priest may touch the ears and mouth of the newly baptized and say ephphatha, praying that they will hear and proclaim God's word; some Christians pray the word for open ears and hearts.

games.q: a crowd brings you a man who can't hear, and begs you to lay your hand on him. what does Jesus do first?
o: lay a hand on his head in front of everyone.
tell him to go and wash.
games.why: he takes him aside from the crowd, touches his ears and tongue, looks up, sighs, and says ephphatha: be opened.

practice: Close your eyes and let the obvious sounds come and pass, then go looking for the hidden ones: the hum of a machine, your own heartbeat, wind against a window, a bird far off.
Pick one and give it your full attention, as if you'd never heard it before. If you pray, you can offer the word to God: ephphatha.

wordCard.voice: Ephphatha. Aramaic for be opened, sighed by Jesus with his fingers in a deaf man's ears.

orig.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters by Mark: be opened.

carryVoice: Your line: a sound you usually ignore. Fingers, a sigh, and ears opened. Twenty-seven weeks, done.
